title: Colitis and Proctitis

content_blocks.text: Colitis—inflammation of the colon (large intestine); colitis may be acute and self-
Colitis does not infer causality, and an underlying cause of the colitis should be investigated, particularly in chronic

Inflammation of the colon causes accumulation of inflammatory cytokines, disrupts tight junctions between epithelial cells, stimulates colonic secretion, stimulates goblet cell secretion of mucus, and disrupts motility.
These mechanisms reduce the ability of the colon to absorb water and electrolytes, and store feces, which causes frequent diarrhea, often with mucus and/or frank blood.
Breeds predisposed to histiocytic ulcerative colitis (granulomatous colitis [GC]) include boxers, French bulldogs, and, less commonly,
German shepherd dogs are predisposed to perianal fistulae (anal furunculosis) that can be associated with colitis.

Histopathologic findings depend on histologic type of colitis—lymphoplasmacytic, eosinophilic, or histiocytic represent most common subtypes; hyperplastic mucosa may be seen with irritable bowel syndrome; various infectious agents may be seen with special stains.

Fiber supplementation with poorly fermented fiber (e.g., bran and alphacellulose) recommended to increase fecal bulk, improve colonic muscle contractility, and bind fecal water to produce formed

Some fermentable fiber sources (e.g., psyllium or diet containing beet pulp or fructooligosaccharides) may be beneficial— short-chain fatty acids produced by fermentation may be beneficial for colonocyte function.

Segments of colon severely affected by fibrosis from chronic inflammation and subsequent stricture formation may need surgical excision, especially in patients with granulomatous form of disease; cecal inversion and ileocecocolic intussusception require surgical intervention; pythiosis/phycomycosis often requires surgical excision or debulking.
